title: USB-C hub or dock? Check these five things before buying
summary: Avoid the wrong ports, display limitations, and charging surprises when connecting a home-office laptop.

sections.title: Map the desk you actually use
paragraphs: Write down the exact laptop model, operating system, monitor model, resolution, and refresh rate you want to use. Then list your peripherals: keyboard, mouse, camera, microphone, storage, Ethernet, and memory cards. Count connections that must work at the same time. A compact hub that solves one portable setup may be the wrong choice for a permanent two-monitor desk.

Keep your existing charger in the plan. A hub with a power-input port does not necessarily include a charger, and a connector that fits does not by itself establish video support, charging output, or data speed. Read the laptop and hub documentation together.

sections.title: 1. Confirm the laptop’s port capabilities
paragraphs: Look up the exact port specification in the manufacturer’s manual. USB-C describes the connector, while the supported functions vary. Confirm video output support if you want an HDMI-connected monitor through a hub. Do not infer Thunderbolt capability from the connector shape.
If you use a work-managed laptop, check whether a dock requires software that your organization allows. A device that depends on a driver may be unsuitable when you cannot install it.

sections.title: 2. Decide on displays before counting USB ports
paragraphs: Choose how many independent screens you need, then verify the combination of laptop, operating system, dock, and monitor. Two sockets on a dock are not a promise of two extended displays on every laptop. Check the supported resolution and refresh rate for the exact connection path.

For a single external display and a few accessories, a portable hub can be enough. For multiple displays or a desk that stays permanently wired, compare docks against the laptop manufacturer’s supported configurations.

sections.title: 3. Budget power, not just advertised wattage
paragraphs: Compare the power delivered to the laptop with its requirements. Input power and laptop output are different numbers because a hub uses some power itself. Confirm the cable and charger requirements as well as the hub specification.

As a concrete example, Anker lists its 555 USB-C Hub (A8383) with up to 100W power input and 85W output to the laptop. That distinction matters more than an isolated “100W” headline. We have not tested this product; check your laptop’s requirements before treating it as a candidate.

sections.title: 4. Check the ports you will share
paragraphs: The Anker A8383 specification lists one HDMI output up to 4K at 60Hz, one USB-C data port, two USB-A data ports, Gigabit Ethernet, and SD and microSD slots. It is a useful example of a single-HDMI hub, not evidence of support for a multi-monitor setup.

Count whether storage, camera, and input devices can stay attached simultaneously. If file transfers are important, check both the drive and hub specifications; advertised port speed is not a guarantee of real-world transfer speed. Avoid buying a hub just because it has the largest port count.

sections.title: 5. Test the complete setup while returns are possible
paragraphs: Connect every device you intend to use. Try a video call while accessing your external drive, then check display wake-up, charging behavior, and reconnecting after sleep. Save your work before disconnecting storage and follow the operating system’s safe-removal process.

Keep a simple pass/fail checklist for your own setup. If your existing connections already work reliably, there may be no reason to upgrade. The goal is fewer connection problems, not a more elaborate desk.
